How to Calculate Your Taxes on a Paycheck

Direct AnswerCalculate taxes on your paycheck step by step for 2026: gross pay, pre-tax deductions, FICA, federal withholding, and state taxes, with real numbers.

Quick Answer

Work in order: start with gross pay, subtract pre-tax deductions, then FICA, then 2026 federal withholding, then state tax — what remains is your net pay.

Few moments in working life are as disorienting as opening a brand-new paycheck. You calculate your hourly rate or annual salary on paper, wait eagerly for payday, and expect a clean round number. But when direct deposit arrives on Friday morning, hundreds of dollars have vanished before reaching your bank account. A pay stub looks like a blur of acronyms: FIT, FICA OASDI, FICA MED, SIT, and Pre-Tax Sec 125.

Workers often assume payroll taxes are a single flat fee or an opaque black box. In reality, paycheck withholdings follow deterministic IRS rules based on gross pay, pre-tax exemptions, statutory payroll contributions, and progressive tax brackets.

In this guide, we walk through an illustrative 5-step framework that shows how each dollar is accounted for on a typical paycheck. We trace a complete real-world example of a $25-an-hour worker paid biweekly, uncover the crucial distinction between 401(k) and health insurance deductions that most calculators get wrong, provide the updated 2026 federal tax brackets, and show you how to audit your own pay stub with complete confidence.

Calculate Your Paycheck

The "Paycheck Shock": Where Does Your Money Actually Go?

When you negotiate an hourly wage or accept an annual salary, you are agreeing to your gross compensation—the total earnings your employer pays before any deductions. But your household budget runs strictly on net take-home pay.

The gap between gross and net earnings is not a single deduction. It is divided into three distinct categories:

1. Pre-Tax Deductions
Voluntary Benefit Contributions

Elective benefits subtracted before taxes: health insurance, dental, vision, HSA/FSA contributions, and Traditional 401(k) retirement plans.

2. Mandatory FICA Taxes
7.65% Federal Payroll Taxes

Statutory federal contributions: 6.2% for Social Security (up to the annual wage cap) plus 1.45% for Medicare on all covered earnings.

3. Income Tax Withholding
Federal, State & Local Taxes

Progressive income taxes withheld based on your Form W-4 elections, standard deduction, filing status, and state of residence.

The 5-Step Paycheck Tax Calculation Framework

To calculate your net take-home paycheck accurately, follow this sequential 5-step payroll formula:

Net Take-Home Pay = Gross Pay − Pre-Tax Deductions − FICA Taxes − Federal Income Tax − State/Local Taxes − Post-Tax Deductions

Every deduction must be calculated in its exact legal sequence to determine accurate taxable wages.

To see how this works in real life, let us walk through a concrete scenario: a single employee earning $25.00 per hour, working 40 hours per week, paid on a biweekly schedule (26 paychecks per year). Compare how this scales with our comprehensive guides on $23 an hour and $45 an hour.

Step 1: Calculate Gross Pay per Paycheck ($25/Hour Example)

Your gross pay is your total earned compensation before any withholdings or voluntary deductions. For an hourly employee, multiply your base hourly wage by the total number of hours worked during the pay period:

Biweekly Gross Pay = Hourly Rate × Hours Worked in Pay Period

$25.00/hour × 80 regular hours = $2,000.00 Gross Biweekly Pay

Across all 26 biweekly pay periods, an employee earning $2,000.00 per check generates an annual gross salary of $52,000.00 ($2,000 × 26). If you are paid semi-monthly (24 checks per year) or monthly (12 checks per year), use our free Hourly Wage Converter to find your exact gross check amount.

Step 2: Subtract Pre-Tax Deductions (Medical vs. 401k Rules)

Pre-tax deductions represent benefits you pay for directly from your paycheck before income taxes are computed. However, here is the critical payroll rule that most websites and generic calculators get wrong: not all pre-tax deductions are treated equally by the IRS!

  • Section 125 "Cafeteria" Plans (Medical, Dental, Vision, HSA, FSA): These deductions are fully exempt from both Federal Income Tax (FIT) and FICA payroll taxes (Social Security and Medicare). When you pay $100 toward health insurance, that $100 is completely invisible to federal, state, and FICA taxes.
  • Retirement Contributions (Traditional 401(k), 403(b), 457): Traditional retirement contributions are exempt from Federal Income Tax (and most state income taxes), but they are still subject to mandatory FICA taxes. You still pay the 7.65% Social Security and Medicare tax on every dollar you save into a 401(k).

For our working example, assume our $25/hour worker elects two standard workplace benefits each biweekly pay period:

  • Employer Health Insurance Premium (Section 125): $100.00 per check
  • Traditional 401(k) Contribution (5% of Gross): $100.00 per check ($2,000 × 5%)
  • Total Pre-Tax Deductions: $200.00 per check

Step 3: Calculate Mandatory FICA Taxes (Social Security & Medicare)

FICA stands for the Federal Insurance Contributions Act. It is a mandatory federal payroll tax split into two programs: Social Security (OASDI) and Medicare (Hospital Insurance). Unlike federal income tax, FICA has no standard deduction or zero-bracket threshold—it applies from your first dollar of wages.

Because Section 125 medical premiums are exempt from FICA, but 401(k) contributions are not, our worker's FICA Taxable Wage Base is:

FICA Taxable Base = Gross Pay − Section 125 Deductions = $2,000.00 − $100.00 = $1,900.00

Now, calculate the two FICA components:

  1. Social Security Tax (6.2%):
    Taxed at 6.2% up to the 2026 Social Security wage base limit of $184,500.
    $1,900.00 × 6.2% = $117.80 per check ($3,062.80 annually).
  2. Medicare Tax (1.45%):
    Taxed at 1.45% on all covered wages without an annual ceiling. (Note: High earners making over $200,000 for single filers pay an Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9%, but that does not apply here).
    $1,900.00 × 1.45% = $27.55 per check ($716.30 annually).
Total Biweekly FICA Taxes = $117.80 + $27.55 = $145.35 per paycheck

Total Annual FICA = $145.35 × 26 paychecks = $3,779.10 per year

Step 4: Calculate 2026 Federal Income Tax Withholding

Federal Income Tax (FIT) withholding is determined using IRS percentage method tables (IRS Publication 15-T) based on your Form W-4 elections. Both Section 125 medical insurance ($100) and Traditional 401(k) contributions ($100) are exempt from Federal Income Tax, giving an Income Taxable Wage Base of $1,800.00 per paycheck ($2,000 − $200).

To calculate biweekly withholding under the IRS Percentage Method for a Single filer claiming the standard deduction:

  1. Annualize Taxable Wages: $1,800.00 per check × 26 pay periods = $46,800.00 annual taxable wages.
  2. Subtract the 2026 Standard Deduction: The IRS standard deduction for single filers is $16,100.00.
    Taxable Income = $46,800.00 − $16,100.00 = $30,700.00.
  3. Apply 2026 Federal Progressive Tax Brackets:
    • 10% on the first $12,400.00 = $1,240.00
    • 12% on the remaining $18,300.00 ($30,700 − $12,400) = $2,196.00
    • Total Annual Federal Income Tax: $1,240.00 + $2,196.00 = $3,436.00
  4. De-Annualize to the Paycheck Level:
    $3,436.00 ÷ 26 pay periods = $132.15 Federal Income Tax per paycheck

Marginal Rate (12%) vs. Effective Federal Tax Rate (6.61%)

While our worker's top dollar falls into the 12% marginal tax bracket, their effective federal tax rate is only 6.61% of their gross income ($3,436 ÷ $52,000). The standard deduction shields the first $16,100 from tax entirely, and the next $12,400 is taxed at only 10%.

2026 Federal Tax Brackets Reference Table (Single & MFJ)

Use this reference table to see the 2026 federal progressive tax brackets for Single filers and Married Filing Jointly (MFJ) after subtracting the standard deduction ($16,100 for Single; $32,200 for MFJ):

Tax Rate Single Filer Taxable Income Married Filing Jointly (MFJ) How the Rate Applies
10% $0 to $12,400 $0 to $24,800 Applies to your first tier of taxable income
12% $12,401 to $50,400 $24,801 to $100,800 Covers the majority of middle-class earnings
22% $50,401 to $105,700 $100,801 to $211,400 Applies to upper-middle individual wages
24% $105,701 to $201,050 $211,401 to $402,100 Professional and upper-tier earnings

Step 5: Account for State & Local Income Taxes

State and local income tax withholdings vary dramatically depending on your geographical location:

  • No-Income-Tax States (0%): If you work in Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, or Wyoming, you pay $0.00 in state income tax on earned wages.
  • Flat-Rate States: Several states levy a simple flat tax across all taxable wages, such as Pennsylvania (3.07%), Indiana (3.05%), Arizona (2.5%), or Illinois (4.95%). On an $1,800 taxable wage, a 4% state tax withholds approximately $72.00 to $76.00 per paycheck.
  • Progressive Tax States: States like California, New York, New Jersey, and Oregon use multi-bracket systems ranging from 1% to over 9%, plus local municipal taxes (such as NYC or Philadelphia city wage taxes).

The Complete Paycheck Breakdown: Gross to Net Pay Table

Here is the complete line-by-line audit of our $25/hour worker's biweekly paycheck, comparing take-home pay in a no-tax state versus a moderate 4% state income tax state:

Paycheck Line Item Category No State Tax (e.g., TX, FL) Moderate 4% State Tax
Gross Biweekly Pay (80 hrs @ $25) Gross Earnings +$2,000.00 +$2,000.00
Health Insurance Premium (Sec 125) Pre-Tax (FIT & FICA exempt) -$100.00 -$100.00
Traditional 401(k) Retirement (5%) Pre-Tax (FIT exempt only) -$100.00 -$100.00
Social Security Tax (6.2% on $1,900) Mandatory FICA -$117.80 -$117.80
Medicare Tax (1.45% on $1,900) Mandatory FICA -$27.55 -$27.55
Federal Income Tax Withholding Mandatory FIT -$132.15 -$132.15
State Income Tax Withholding State Tax (SIT) $0.00 -$76.00
Net Take-Home Pay (Direct Deposit) Net Cash $1,522.50 $1,446.50

In a state with no income tax, our worker keeps $1,522.50 per biweekly paycheck (76.1% of gross earnings). In a state with a 4% income tax, take-home pay is $1,446.50 per paycheck (72.3% of gross earnings). Test your own paycheck numbers with our free Paycheck Calculator.

Why Bonuses and Overtime Checks Seem Taxed Higher

Workers frequently complain that bonuses or heavy overtime checks get "eaten by taxes." This phenomenon is driven by two specific payroll mechanics:

  1. The 22% Flat Supplemental Withholding Rule: The IRS permits employers to withhold a flat 22% federal tax on supplemental income (bonuses, commissions, awards). If your regular marginal bracket is only 10% or 12%, this flat 22% rate makes your bonus check feel severely penalized.
  2. The Annualization Illusion on Overtime Checks: Payroll software calculates tax on each individual check by multiplying that check's earnings across the full year. If you pick up 20 hours of overtime and your gross check jumps from $2,000 to $3,000, the software assumes you earn $78,000 all year long and withholds tax at a higher rate for that specific pay cycle.

The Reality at Tax Time: Withholding is only an estimate. When you file your annual Form 1040 tax return, all your income is combined. If too much tax was withheld from your bonus or overtime checks, every single overpaid dollar is returned to you as an income tax refund.

Common Form W-4 Mistakes That Distort Your Paycheck

Your employer's payroll software relies directly on the information you submit on IRS Form W-4. Watch out for these three common mistakes:

Mistake 1: Leaving Step 2 blank when you or your spouse work multiple jobs.

If you work two jobs or are married filing jointly with a working spouse, both employers assume you are their only source of income and apply full standard deductions. Check the box in Step 2(c) or use the multiple jobs worksheet to prevent an unexpected tax bill in April.

Mistake 2: Claiming child tax credits twice on two separate W-4 forms.

The Child Tax Credit ($2,000 per qualifying child) should only be claimed on one W-4 form in Step 3—usually the highest-earning job. Splitting or duplicating credits across two jobs results in under-withholding.

Mistake 3: Never updating your W-4 after life transitions.

Marriage, divorce, purchasing a home, having a child, or picking up freelance income all change your tax liability. Review your W-4 annually to ensure your paycheck withholding matches your financial goals.

Frequently Asked Questions About Paycheck Taxes

How do I calculate the taxes taken out of my paycheck?

To calculate the taxes taken out of your paycheck, start with your gross earnings for the pay period and subtract qualifying pre-tax deductions (such as health insurance and traditional 401k) to find your taxable wages. Next, calculate FICA taxes: Social Security (6.2% of gross pay up to the $184,500 wage cap in 2026) and Medicare (1.45% of all gross pay). Then, determine federal income tax withholding using IRS Publication 15-T based on your Form W-4 filing status. Finally, add state and local income tax withholdings. Subtracting total taxes and any post-tax deductions from your gross pay yields your net take-home pay.

Does traditional 401(k) reduce Social Security and Medicare taxes?

No. Traditional 401(k) and 403(b) contributions reduce your federal and state income taxable wages, but they do NOT reduce your FICA taxes (Social Security and Medicare). FICA taxes are calculated on your gross wages before retirement contributions are deducted. In contrast, Section 125 cafeteria benefits—such as employer-sponsored medical, dental, and vision insurance premiums—reduce both income taxes and FICA taxes.

Why is my take-home pay so much less than my salary?

Your take-home pay is significantly lower than your gross salary because employers are legally required to withhold mandatory statutory taxes and optional benefit deductions from every paycheck. These deductions typically include federal income tax withholding (usually 10% to 22% for most workers), FICA payroll taxes (7.65% combined for Social Security and Medicare), state and local income taxes (ranging from 0% to over 9%), health insurance premiums, and retirement contributions. Together, these line items often consume between 20% and 32% of your gross earnings.

Will working overtime put me in a higher tax bracket and make me lose money?

No, this is a common myth. The United States uses a progressive marginal tax bracket system. When you earn extra overtime pay and cross into a higher tax bracket, only the specific dollars earned above that bracket threshold are taxed at the higher percentage rate. Every dollar earned below that threshold continues to be taxed at lower bracket rates. You will always take home more money overall by working overtime, even if slightly more tax is withheld from that specific check.

Why was my bonus taxed at a higher rate than my normal paycheck?

Bonuses and supplemental wages are often subjected to a flat 22% federal supplemental withholding rate by employer payroll systems, regardless of your normal tax bracket. If your typical marginal tax rate is only 10% or 12%, this creates the illusion of a massive penalty on payday. However, when you file your annual tax return, your bonus is simply added to your total annual taxable income, and any excess withholding is refunded to you.

How can I change how much tax is withheld from my paycheck?

File a new Form W-4 with your employer — you can do this at any time, not just at hiring. To reduce withholding, claim the dependents and other credits you qualify for in Step 3; to increase withholding (for example, to cover a side income), enter an extra amount per pay period in Step 4(c). Most employers apply the change within one or two pay periods. If you are unsure of the right amount, use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator and then check the result against your next pay stub.

Key Takeaways & Paycheck Audit Checklist

Paycheck Tax Calculation Checklist

  • Sequential Withholding: Taxes are calculated after subtracting qualifying pre-tax benefits from gross pay.
  • FICA Rules: Section 125 medical deductions reduce FICA taxes; 401(k) contributions do not.
  • Effective vs. Marginal: Your marginal bracket reflects only your highest dollar; your effective federal tax rate is substantially lower.
  • W-4 Accuracy: Keep your W-4 updated to prevent unexpected tax bills or excess refunds.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Pre-tax deductions, such as 401(k) contributions and medical premiums, lower the pay that tax is calculated on.
  2. FICA and federal withholding are separate lines — FICA covers Social Security and Medicare, while federal withholding follows the 2026 brackets.
  3. State tax is the last step and it varies by state, so the federal steps alone do not give your final take-home pay.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated October 17, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
